edits.lead_in: Which of the following is the most appropriate cervical cancer screening plan?

edits.html:
Cervical Screening: the Age-21 Floor

Screening eligibility depends on age, not on individual risk

Source vignette Pt — 20 yo F, sexual debut at 15, five lifetime partners, inconsistent condom use · Q — the most appropriate screening step; options spanned no screening until 21, cytology now and co-testing now
The decision point

A 20-year-old is below the screening floor. Sexual debut at 15, five partners and inconsistent condom use each raise HPV (human papillomavirus) exposure, but none of them lowers the starting age. She needs no cytology; screening begins at 21.

The age floor deliberately ignores individual risk. HPV infection in adolescents is near-universal and clears in ~90% within 2 years. Progression to cancer takes more than a decade, so cervical cancer under 21 is rare. Early screening finds transient infection and leads to excisional procedures (LEEP, loop electrosurgical excision procedure) that raise preterm-birth risk in women who were never going to develop cancer. Screening her would cause harm without benefit.

Cervical screening — age gates
AgeScreen withInterval
<21Do not screen — regardless of sexual history, partners, or STI (sexually transmitted infection) history—
21–29Cytology aloneEvery 3 years
30–65Cytology q3y · co-testing q5y · primary HPV q5y3 or 5 years
>65Stop if adequate prior negative screening and no CIN2+ (cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 or worse) in 25 years—
⚠︎ Primary HPV start age Exam answer: primary HPV (human papillomavirus) testing from age 30, per question banks and the USPSTF (US Preventive Services Task Force).
Clinical practice: the 2020 ACS (American Cancer Society) guideline prefers primary HPV testing from age 25, every 5 years.
Answer 30 on the exam.
Exit ramps: where the schedule changes HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) infection → start at 21 as usual, or at diagnosis if older; cytology yearly, and after 3 normal annual results every 3 years (HHS (Department of Health and Human Services) 2024, reviewed 2026; ASCCP (American Society for Colposcopy and Cervical Pathology) 2026). Note: the CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) 2021 STI guideline still says 1 year after sexual debut, no later than 21; current HHS and ASCCP guidance (start at 21) sets the answer · other immunocompromise (organ or allogeneic stem cell transplant, immunosuppressed inflammatory bowel disease) → start at 21, then the same accelerated schedule · in-utero DES (diethylstilbestrol) exposure → annual · prior CIN2+ (cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 or worse) → surveillance every 3 years for 25 years, including past 65 · hysterectomy with cervix removed for benign disease → stop entirely · cervix retained (supracervical) → keep screening · vaccinated → schedule unchanged.
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
AgeFirstAge under 21, with or without HIVNo screening, whatever the sexual history
Cytology, age 21 to 24ScreenASC-USRepeat cytology in 1 year, or reflex HPV; HPV negative resumes routine
Co-test, age 30 or olderScreenCytology negative, HPV positive not 16 or 18Repeat co-test in 1 year
HPV genotypingBy branchHPV 16 or 18Colposcopy now
Colposcopy with directed biopsyConfirmsCIN grade on histologyConfirms the abnormal screen; CIN2 or worse is treated
Biopsy of a visible lesionConfirmsDysplasia or invasive carcinomaDiagnostic at any age, including under 21
Cytology or HPV test before 21SkipHPV clears in about 90% within 2 yearsFinds transient infection and leads to excisions that raise preterm-birth risk
Scenario bank
  1. 20 yo F, debut at 15, five partners → No screening → begin at 21
  2. 18 yo F seen to start care 2 weeks after a positive HIV test; sexually active since 15 with two lifetime partners, uses condoms inconsistently; T 36.8 °C, BP 112/70 mm Hg; pelvic examination normal → Begin at 21 as usual → HIV does not lower the start age; from 21, cytology yearly, then every 3 years after 3 normal results
  3. 21 yo F, virgin, never sexually active → Screen anyway; the recommendation is age-based, not activity-based
  4. 24 yo F with ASC-US cytology → Reflex HPV; if negative, resume routine
  5. 28 yo F, normal cytology 2 years ago → Return in 1 year → every 3 years from the last test
  6. 33 yo F, cytology negative / HPV positive, not 16 or 18 → Repeat co-test in 1 year
  7. 33 yo F, cytology negative / HPV 16 positive → Colposcopy → genotype escalates
  8. 67 yo F, three consecutive negatives, no CIN history → Stop screening
  9. 67 yo F with CIN2 treated 10 years ago → Keep screening → the 25-year clock overrides age 65
  10. 42 yo F, hysterectomy for fibroids, cervix removed → Stop · hysterectomy for cervical cancer → continue vaginal cuff cytology
  11. 20 yo F with visible cervical lesion or postcoital bleeding → Biopsy the lesion → that's diagnostic, not screening
Distractors Her risk history: a salient decoy that makes "no screening" feel negligent.
Colposcopy: a sequencing trap; it is for an abnormal result, and she has no result.
HPV vaccination counseling (HPV: human papillomavirus): a true-fact-wrong-slot. At 20 she is within catch-up vaccination, which runs through 26, so it is indicated. It does not answer the screening question.
Pairs with Part I Cervical Cancer Screening (interval mechanics when cytology and co-testing fall out of sync) and HPV Vaccination & Series Rules. Ask: "Is she eligible yet?" before "Is she at risk?"
Transferable rule Screening guidelines are population rules with age gates. Individual risk factors adjust intensity within the eligible window; they rarely move the floor. Check eligibility before you calculate risk.
